I'm a computational biologist with a PhD in Genetics & Molecular Biology from Emory University. I came to coding as a biologist first — self-taught, R-native, Python when the job calls for it — now through AI I suppose. I spent my graduate work turning large, multi-omic sequencing datasets into answers about how the adaptive immune system is regulated transcriptionally and epigenetically, or **disregulated in the case of autoimmunity**.

Most of my work from the last few years is in **spatial transcriptomics**: building analysis pipelines for imaging-based platforms like 10x Xenium, benchmarking cell segmentation algorithms, and developing methods to measure when segmentation gets it wrong. I also do odds and ends supporting our group's work on delivery for mRNA-based therapuetics. This includes guide selection for Cas9 systems, single-cell, or bulk genomic datasets.

Now I run all of my groups computational functions. That means managing a few over-powered workstations, a team of over-eager AI agentic assistants, and developing Claude skills to enable our lab scientists to run their own pipelines to analyze their data directly. 

## What I work on

- **Spatial transcriptomics** — end-to-end Xenium analysis: alternative segmentation, QC, tissue microarray processing, and downstream spatial statistics
- **Method development** — [CRISP](software.qmd), a software package for assessing cell segmentation quality using co-expression of mutually exclusive markers
- **Single-cell and bulk genomics** — RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, integration, and gene regulatory network analysis
- **Reproducible pipelines** — Nextflow and R-based workflows designed so the next person (often future me) can rerun them
- **AI-based bioinformatics** — learning how to use agents for data anlysis in responsible and reproducible ways (see [Stringency](https://github.com/santangelo-lab/stringency))
